title: Raised by the river
hookLine: a king's daughter is raised by fishermen, and the epic's own answer to what makes a person
carry: conduct, not birth, shows who you are

lines: A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.
cards: A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell.
He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river.
This is where Satyavati's story begins.

teach.b: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls.

Some time later, fishermen catch her, and inside they find two human children, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends, and she rises back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king, and the king makes a choice.
He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be King Matsya.
The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen: let her be your daughter. She grows up on the river, carrying the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati.
Remember what she told Shantanu: I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen. Every word true. Now see where the poem takes her.

teach.h: A FISHER GIRL BECOMES A QUEEN.
teach.b: This fisher girl becomes a queen of the Kurus, and the great-grandmother of the cousins the great war is about. Her first son will be Vyasa, the sage Hindus honor for arranging the Vedas and telling this very epic.
Many teachers point to it: the greatest teacher in the story is a fisherwoman's son. And the epic says it outright, later on.
A serpent asks Prince Yudhishthira who is truly a Brahmin.
His answer: look for truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct. If those are in someone born low and missing in someone born high, birth doesn't decide it.
India's history has also ranked people by birth, by caste, and that has done real harm; many Hindu saints and reformers have pushed back, pointing to stories like these.

how: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

games.q: your cousin says Vyasa can't be that great, his mom was a fisher girl. by the epic's own teaching, what fits?
o: the epic weighs conduct over birth. its great sage came from the river.
he's right: a great sage needs a high-born mother.
it doesn't matter, it's only a story.
games.why: Satyavati was raised among fishermen, and her son became the sage Hindus thank for the Vedas. Yudhishthira says it plainly later: look at conduct, not birth.

practice: In many Hindu rites, the priest asks your name and your gotra, your family line. Today, say your own line quietly: your name, then the people who raised you, by blood or by love, as far back as you know.
Then add one quality you want people to find in you: truth, patience, kindness. In this epic, that counts too.

wordCard.voice: Satyavati. A king's daughter raised as a fisherman's own, and mother of the sage the Vedas come through.

orig.note: Sanskrit Satyavatī, the name of the girl the fishermen's chief raised: later a queen of the Kurus.

carryVoice: Your line: conduct, not birth, shows who you are. Tomorrow, a boat on the river, and the son born on an island. Day seven hundred sixteen, done.
